Topic: “It Don’t Mean a Thing If It Ain’t Got That Swing: Popular Music and Dance.” From the Charleston to “Hot to Go,” this course will provide students with an understanding of how popular music and iconic dances progress from marginalized communities to mainstream culture in the United States. Through critical case studies, students will get to know how racial and gender identities shape the creation and reception of music genres and dance trends, develop the skills to critically discuss and write about the intertextual relationship between sound and movement, and examine how media extracts practices from marginalized communities and reframe them to be accepted by mainstream American culture.

Rubber Soul: Race, Genre, and the Sonic Politics of Rock ‘n’ Roll Rock music is Black music. Evolving out of the blues and, later, rhythm and blues, rock ‘n’ roll circa 1950s to early 1960s had a Black face, with artists like Chuck Berry and Little Richard leading the way. Yet, as rock ‘n’ roll gave way to rock during the second half of the 1960s, its Black origins were obscured, and rock culture became predominantly white. What were the cultural, historical, and sonic traditions that made rock ‘n’ roll possible? How did the erasure of Blacks from rock happen and why? What were the financial and cultural implications of that erasure? Students will learn about rock ‘n’ roll history, with an emphasis on rock from the 1960s and 1970s. Beginning in the 1920s and 1930s, with the sounds of delta and classic blues (Charley Patton, Bessie Smith) and early country too (Jimmie Rodgers, Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys), we will trace the arc of rock ‘n’ roll to rock, culminating with post-punk and the early-1980s, MTV era, second British Invasion (Duran Duran, Culture Club). Students will have the opportunity to write a short piece of rock criticism and a final seminar paper and presentation about a rock artist or an element of rock culture.

The Sacred Harp: the Performance and Politics of Shape-Note Singing Sacred Harp is a style of shape-note singing with histories in the American South and 18th– 19th century New England and the Mid-Atlantic. This class explores the complex histories, meanings, and performance of Sacred Harp and shape-note singing. Classes are divided between lecture-discussions and learning to sing Sacred Harp music in the traditional manner.

sections.note: Black Music and Culture of the 1970s: The 1970s was—and remains—a key time period for understanding Black American musical and social life. This course will examine works by artists like Stevie Wonder, Aretha Franklin, and Marvin Gaye to understand the main musical ideas and social concerns of these artists and their audiences. Reading, listening, and discussion will focus on issues including the Civil Rights and Black Power movements, deindustrialization, technology, and the music industry. Our goal will be to build research and writing skills while studying this period. With our understanding of soul, funk, disco, jazz, and the beginnings of hip-hop, our final question will be: how and to what extent can we hear echoes of the Black music and culture of the 1970s in later decades and in our contemporary era?

sections.note: Topic: "WOMEN IN MUSIC, PRE-1650." Explores women's musical activities from the late Middle Ages to about 1650, demonstrating how women shaped some of the most celebrated musical traditions of these centuries. Five units examine (1) women in premodern court cultures; (2) women in religious institutions; (3) women as patrons; (4) women as subjects of compositions; and (5) women in early opera. The course focuses on European figures, with comparative case studies from elsewhere in Eurasia and the wider Mediterranean. Some case studies include queer or queer-coded identities and works, approached with attention to how understandings of sexuality change across cultures and time. Designed for advanced undergraduates and graduate students. Open to students across campus; music-reading ability is not required. Unit 1 includes discussion of sex work; alternative assignments available on request.

Musical Theatre Repertoire is an asynchronous course delivered through GoReact, an interactive, video-based platform that allows student to submit performances and receive individualized feedback. Throughout the course, students will explore a broad range of musical theatre styles and genres, including Jazz Age, Golden Age, comedic and character repertoire, Sondheim, Disney, and pop/rock. Weekly feedback will address vocal technique, musical and stylistic choices, interpretive skills, and effective communication of text, with an emphasis on developing versatile, informed, and expressive musical theatre performers.

Topic: "BLACK SACRED MUSIC SYMPOSIUM XX." Instruction and experience in the performance of Black Sacred Music traditions such as congregational singing, folk and concert spirituals, metered and improvised hymns, anthems, and traditional and contemporary gospel songs. Topics include history and development, choral pedagogy, conducting, song selection, and vocal and instrumental performance techniques. Additionally, participants attend musical rehearsals and perform the repertoire learned during Symposium in a closing concert. The Eighteenth Black Sacred Music Symposium will be Thursday-Sunday, February 25-28, 2027.

Topic: "ENSEMBLE CREDIT - COLLABORATIVE PIANO AND CHAMBER MUSIC." Pianists only. Pianists work with ensembles, classes, and/or performances in the School of Music. Instructor Approval required, please see Dr. Chi-Chen Wu.

This course is designed to introduce and develop the essential skills for work as a music director in productions for the contemporary musical stage and high-level freelance work. Students will learn the rudiments of arranging and improvisation from a harmonic skeleton, become acquainted with the use of computers and stand-alone synthesizers, develop the skill of conducting from the keyboard, and attain basic familiarity with contemporary and classical musical theater vocal and instrumental styles. Students will prepare a musical to teach the class applying in a practical manner the skills studied. Excerpts from this musical will also be arranged for vocal and variable instrumental ensembles.

Topic: "ENSEMBLE CREDIT FOR PIANISTS - CHAMBER MUSIC AND ACCOMPANYING." Purpose of course / learning outcome: To actively participate in ensemble playing as a pianist, learning the associated skills, protocol and repertoire for specific use in collaborative settings including chamber music, vocal accompanying, choral accompanying, orchestral piano, dance class accompaniment or other activities as assigned. Procedures: In consultation with the instructor and other SoM or related faculty, the student will be assigned an activity. Examples: accompany a choir in rehearsal and performance, observe dance classes and then play classes at the instructor and supervisor’s discretion, accompany for a weekly voice lesson and select public performances with the singer, accompany for a portion of a solo degree recital or studio recital, participate as the pianist in an orchestra or band for one or more concerts and the appropriate rehearsals, etc.

It is not intended to replace semester-long diction courses for students in the Vocal Performance or Vocal Coaching and Accompanying degrees. Using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), students will learn accurate and fluent pronunciation in the five primary singing languages (Italian, German, French, Latin, and English). In addition, they will develop their ear to recognize and correct pronunciation issues in their own and others' singing.

Topic: Teaching Instrumental Music in Fieldwork Settings This course provides students with supervised teaching experiences in instrumental music fieldwork settings. Students engage with learners and community partners through the planning, implementation, and assessment of music instruction. Emphasis is placed on developing responsive and inclusive teaching practices, adapting instruction to varied learners and contexts, structuring and leading creative musical activities, and reflecting on emergent teacher identities. Students connect field experiences to current theories and practices in music education through guided reflection, reading, and discussion.

Topic: "SPANISH DICTION." Fundamentals of Spanish diction, designed for voice majors, but open to other music majors and non-music majors. The course will cover the basics of IPA (International Phonetic Alphabet) as applied to the Spanish language.

The year 1927 will be the focal point for a wide-ranging seminar-style exploration of musical issues in America and Europe. A broad introduction will be followed by weekly case studies in which representative compositions and recordings help to bring key issues into focus: the clash and blend of musical idioms viewed as “high” and “low,” the impact of new technology (radio, sound film, electric recording) on musical creation and dissemination, machine aesthetics, urbanization, racial representations and assumptions; the co-existing aesthetics of neoclassicism, serialism, neue Sachlichkeit, varieties of American modernism, jazz, blues, spirituals, Broadway, popular song, and the Harlem Renaissance. Readings, listening, and discussion will drive class meetings, culminating in a final research project that intersects meaningfully with the year 1927.

“Sound and Coloniality” takes as its foundation an understanding of coloniality as the formations of knowledge and subjectivity, hierarchies, and social relations that sustain, reproduce, and outlast the colonial structures that generate them. The seminar draws on historical musicology, cultural history, sound studies, material culture, and decolonial studies to generate analytical frameworks to examine how colonized subjects negotiate, contest, appropriate and transform colonial systems through sonic and musical practices. The seminar welcomes participants from across disciplines interested in the critical study of sound and music; proficiency in musical notation or performance is not required.

title: Seminar in Works of Select Composer

sections.note: Benjamin Britten envisioned music as emerging from the active participation of composers, performers, and audiences. In this course, we will explore the relationships Britten forged with these parties as well as his patrons and publishers on both sides of the Atlantic and the so-called “Iron Curtain;” the influences he gleaned from England, Europe, and East Asia; and the reception of his work including the controversies that arose after his death.

Considers music education research within a wider political and social context and addresses some of the dilemma and choices faced when designing and conducting research. Explores different approaches and considers theoretical and methodological issues relevant to the design and conduct of music education research. Students are expected to design a research project that will make a distinct contribution to knowledge and afford evidence of originality, either by the discovery of new evidence, or by the exercise of independent critical judgments. Prerequisite: MUS 533 or equivalent, or consent of instructor.

The course is designed to help prepare graduate students in the School of Music for careers in post-secondary education. It explores the culture of contemporary colleges and universities, a variety of professional roles that shape music in those contexts, the impact of rapid change in higher education, and the resultant need for versatility, adaptability, collaboration, critical thinking, communication, and institutional citizenship. The format will include lecture and discussion, written and oral exercises and assignments, active, weekly class engagement by all, and a variety of guests bringing unique perspectives on the culture and organization of music in higher education. The 4-credit option also requires a substantial final project.

Intended for prospective university teachers of undergraduate music education majors. Covers educational philosophy, curriculum design, methods of teaching and evaluation, and student teaching and observational experiences as they relate to undergraduate music teacher preparation. Prerequisite: Graduate standing in music education; at least three years of public school music teaching experience is highly recommended.
